column1: For over half a century Portsmouth has taken pride in calling itself the “City of the Open Door.” After living in the city for almost four decades

column1: There’s an ad circulating currently on social media — paid for by a group called “Preserve Portsmouth” — that features an unattractively composed photo of an unfinished section of housing in the West End Yards project and asks people: “Do you want to turn Portsmouth into this?” The “this” happens to be the homes of people who have moved or are moving into town. More than likely these newcomers are very happy to be here and have a place like Portsmouth to call home. The ad supports the re-election of Mayor Becksted
column2: councilors Huda
column3: Kennedy
column4: Trace
column5: and Whelan

column7: but their names are there. This is not the voice of the “City of the Open Door.” It’s the opposite of the welcome mat. We have a real housing crisis in our city. We need housing for all. More than ever

column9: including reformed zoning ordinances
column10: that is pro-housing and manages growth through smart land use.

column1: Four years ago during a public session to consider the final phase of development in the North End business
column2: residential
column3: and hotel district
column4: our mayor — then prospective councilor Rick Becksted — stated that he thought “our beautiful city [had] disappeared.” I have no doubt at all that in conveying a sense of loss his comment was heartfelt. But if he’s talking about the city’s physical landscape
column5: he’s been living in a different city than I have. What I’ve seen disappear are large tracts of asphalt parking lots left behind by urban renewal and open weed-covered lots. We can have different ideas about the importance of building height being two
column6: three
column7: or four stories. We can argue about aesthetics. But to my knowledge we haven’t sacrificed a single historic building to new projects. In fact
column8: our stock of historic buildings has probably never been in better shape
column9: often renovated by newcomers and insulated for the 21st century. The changes have also added to our tax base during a time when we lost over $90 million of taxable value when the Schiller Power Station was deregulated and sold. You may think your taxes are high now
column10: they would be higher still without the revenues created by new projects.

column1: Combined
column2: the sentiments of Mayor Becksted and MacDonald provide an insight into the mindset of the mayor’s majority voting bloc on the current council. It also explains the motivation for many of the mayor’s recent ideological appointments to the land use boards
column3: all supported by his voting bloc consisting of Councilors Huda
column4: Kennedy
column5: Whelan
column6: and Trace. They haven’t given the housing issue priority. In fact
column7: since they took office
column8: there’s been a proposed moratorium on housing development
column9: some of them have tried to delay (at the expense of the city’s largest nonprofit) a much-needed affordable public housing project
column10: and they’ve intervened in land use processes — speaking “as residents” — to stall or block specific projects that would provide housing. Pro-housing policy-making should have been the first order of business when the current council term began.

column1: Portsmouth is of course far more than its buildings; it has character and a social fabric. It has a collective way of life
column2: a quilt made up of unique neighborhoods
column3: each with its own personality. And the city has a larger identity that is constantly evolving
column4: something I’ve witnessed in my time here. For some residents
column5: like the mayor
column6: the rate of rapid change has brought with it a sense of something lost. And it’s true that the old social fabric has in some cases grown thinner -- new buildings have appeared and new people have moved into the neighborhoods. While residents may be happy with the increase they’ve seen in the value of their homes
column7: it’s also easy to imagine how change could create fault lines and disorientation in the community. It’s not difficult to see how gentrification rubs both ways: older homes are renovated and streets improved
column8: but something older and familiar has gone. Maybe that’s what the mayor meant. We all have to respect that sentiment but it shouldn’t derail us from creating a different vision. We can’t stop the march of time. A new identity is emerging and we have the chance to shape it with intention.
